children.text: This is Latino USA. The radio journal of news and culture.
I'm Maria Hinojosa, reporting from New York. On this special edition of Latino USA,

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: we remember those who have lost their lives in the last few days in this new, more insecure United States. I don't know. I feel like we lost so many lives for nothing and many families that lost their loved ones.
I love my family so much that I just don't know what to say. It's just-- it's a pain. A deep pain that will never be healed.

Although the attacks came from the air, there's a new focus on security on the US border. If I were a bad guy, I wouldn't invest in a ballistic missile. I would put it in a truck, I would put it in a container, I would put it in a vessel, and I'd simply sail it in across the border. And coming up, a youth commentary. This and more on this edition of Latino USA.

I'm Maria Martin and this is news from Latino USA. In every corner of the country and over innumerable long distance telephone lines, only one thing was being discussed in the last few days. We open this edition of the program with snatch fragments of that discussion, beginning with a place many went to find solace, in church.

It is very hard. And I thank the Lord that we're okay. And we're going to be okay, because it's in the midst of all this that he will take care of everything. This should never happen to the people in the United States. This is a country that has open arms, have received lots of immigrants just like me. And this should have never happened. Our hearts and our thoughts goes to the people that suffered the loss of their loved ones.
Now, voices from the workplace. In Northwest Washington, DC, not far from the capital, Latino USA's Deepa Donde visited the Loriol Plaza, a Mexican-Brazilian restaurant.

There, she spoke with co-owner Luis Reyes, who's originally from El Salvador. Well, I've been really sad since yesterday. Really, really horrible. And I'll be honest, I cry when I find out what happens. And there's no words to describe what is my feeling. I never seen something like this. We had earthquakes all over but this is horrible. I've been living here for a long time and I love this country.

Latino USA also spoke with a waitress named Christina, originally from Bolivia. When I started taking my tables, I didn't know how to approach to my customers. I just want to cry. I feel like we lost so many lives for nothing, and many families that lost their loved ones. I love my family so much that I just-- I just don't know what to say. It's just-- it's a pain. A deep pain that will never be healed.

Everywhere people flock to blood banks in hopes of doing something, anything, any action that would constitute a response to the unimaginable. Well, I'm here today to donate some blood. And I know it's really tragedy over there. It's just-- I got a friend live over there, and I hope he's all right. I'm trying to get in touch with him. So Yasser Arafat went on his own PR blitz today. He actually donated blood to the Americans hurt in the attack. He'll be sending that to the United States.

Also, the Israeli-- I never donated blood before, and I'm a little afraid of needles, so I'm going to stick through it. I'm going to overcome it because I see people needed help. So I really didn't comprehend what was going on until I saw it happen like in the morning, but not until about 2 o'clock did I really realized how many people died. So it kind of hit me. And I had my best friend's dad passed away yesterday too. So yesterday is a bad day, so I want to go help out in any way I can.

Latino media outlets made a major contribution to the discussion. In some instances, abandoning their format entirely. In New York, 97.9 FM La Mega is usually the city's hottest station for musica tropical, but beginning with the first moments of the disaster, it switched over to community news and information full time. This, despite that its FM broadcast towers were located on top of the World Trade Center, their AM station continued broadcasting. Jay Perez is one of the best known voices on Radio La Mega.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: Jay Perez says the station will be here serving the community as long as it is necessary. Normally, we would be broadcasting a music program, but nobody wants to hear music right now. For our community, music generally reflects happiness and celebration. With all that has happened, nobody feels like celebrating. From Austin, Texas, for Latino USA, I'm Maria Martin.
We now return you to the streets surrounding ground zero in Lower Manhattan with our host, Maria Hinojosa.

I'm Maria Hinojosa, and for this show, we are taping in the streets of New York City. In fact, we're in front of Penn Station, another New York landmark. As this program goes to air, there was still no official death toll from the horrific attacks in New York City and Washington, DC.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: It was New York Mayor Rudolph Giuliani who stated what most people already feared, that the death toll would be more than any of us can bear. The terrorists who attacked the Pentagon and the World Trade Center did not discriminate in their deadly actions. Those who perished by them included corporate and military leaders, waiters and busboys, mothers and fathers.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: One person who barely missed being a statistic in New York is Arnulfo Chino, a native of Mexico who's worked his way up from dishwasher to waiter at the World Trade Center. Latino USA's Michelle Garcia actually interviewed him for the first time last month for a report on the growing Mexican presence in New York. That program was originally scheduled to air this week as part of our special Hispanic Heritage Month programming. In the wake of the events of September 11, Latino USA reporters Michele Garcia and Cynthia Rodriguez checked in with him, and they prepared this report.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: Every day for over 10 years, Arnulfo Chino has made the hour long commute from the South Bronx to Lower Manhattan to work. It was morning rush hour in August when we set off down the subway tunnel. 30-year-old Arnulfo slings his uniform fresh from the cleaners over his husky shoulders. Now we are right on the World Trade Center Plaza. You see, everybody is running, everybody is in a hurry, everybody is going to work and wow, it's a crazy city.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: We joined the armies of florists, coffee vendors, store clerks and executives. And of course, it's all office people work around here. As you can see, we got the three World financial center. That's the American Express building, the Lehman Brothers. This place is beautiful. It's nice.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: But we're headed to the Hudson River Club, a three star restaurant where Arnulfo worked his way up from busboy to waiter. He still remembers how awestruck he felt those early years roaming within the massive towers. We walk into the plush restaurant overlooking the harbor, waiters and cooks are busy preparing for the noon crowd. Hey, Carlos. Hey.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: That was what Arnulfo's day should have started like on September the 11, greeting these friends and coworkers. But on this day, two hijacked airplanes pierced the Twin Towers, sending them down into New York's financial center, sending terror, panic, and pain through its people.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: I was thinking of my coworkers. They were my family for 10 years. Five, six Mexicans, they work in the morning. They do the preparations for lunch time, so they start working since 7 o'clock in the morning. And I tried to reach some of them, and I didn't know anything. And we don't know yet what happened with the others.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: Only one night has passed since the attack, and Arnulfo now speaks with a quiet resolve, but desperate to get the details of that morning off his chest. From a Manhattan street corner, he gestures South to where the World Trade Center used to dominate the skyline, and describes what he saw after he emerged from the subway tunnel.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: And then I started looking at the buildings it was horrible. As you can see, the persons, they were jumping out of buildings. So I saw about six, seven people there, they jumping. When it began to rain chunks of metal and glass. So then as soon as I see the buildings, they coming down, the tower coming down, I try to run away, but the other direction, by the Statue of Liberty, all the way down. So I'm running like crazy. As soon as you can see the whole street, you can see people running, yelling. Just like I told you before, I just running away trying to save my life like the other people.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: But it's hard. There's debris falling. Smoke and soot engulfs him. But after two minutes, I see a door was open. The one was at the basement of that building. So then we're running right away, like 30, 35 people. We jump into the room. We get in and then somebody was closed the door and say, no, no more people. And you can hear outside was a lot of people screaming, help. Please open it. Help, help. And nobody can do anything. And they say, no, no, we are so many here, we're going to die. But at that moment, I really think I'm going to die because I cannot even breathe, I cannot even see. That was horrible, believe me.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: Arnulfo's oval face collapses and a look of helplessness even now. He doesn't know what happened to them. Maybe they found a safe place. Maybe they're among the still untold number of casualties among the thousands buried or lost. By six or seven minutes later, we can see a light which is maybe the smoke start go away. You can see the lights. And then we see a glass. So we break the glass, the window, and then we start jumping out of there. And then as soon as we get out, I running away all the way down by South seaport. And everybody was running like crazy trying to save our lives.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: Now, 36 hours later, a heavy metallic stench still envelops the city. People walk around with face masks. Sometimes it's hard to breathe. And we retreat into a nearby community center where Arnulfo normally teaches classes. Arnulfo's worried parents in Southern Mexico have finally gone through on the telephone. Like so many other friends and families, they have desperately been trying to reach their loved ones. Many still search, but the phones have been jammed, making contact difficult. Arnulfo returns from the conversation even more shaken. My mom, she's crying and everything. She told me, what are you doing there, son? Come on over here. Come over here because in Mexico also you can work. So come back with your family. I don't know what you're doing there. Believe me, that was, I don't know, I got to think about it. Believe me.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: Arnulfo Chino doesn't want his parents to worry. But he's a New Yorker now, and just like the others, he will have to find a way to rebuild. For Latino USA with Cynthia Rodriguez, I'm Michelle Garcia, reporting from New York.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: Although terrorists were clearly targeting symbols of American wealth and power, New York City is not only the great American city, it may be the most international city in the world. A place where people from around the world come together. As we heard with the story of Arnulfo Chino, there's also a strong tie between Mexico and the city of New York. Our next report comes from Mexico City and Latino USA's Franc Contreras.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: All across Mexico, from the villages to the largest cities, most Mexicans are expressing a deep sense of disgust at the violent attacks on New York and Washington and their solidarity with the American people. It is a terror. It is a terror. Terror.

On a busy Mexico City street corner, Concepcion Moreno and her husband, Vicente Garcia, are reading newspaper headlines telling of the alliance the US is creating to hunt down the terrorists. When the hijacked jets struck their targets, this couple feared for the safety of their family members living in New York City. They call the attack a crime that can never be justified.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: The Mexican consulate in New York initially reported that 11 Mexicans were hospitalized and at least nine were missing. Juan Cazares, President of New York's Mexican community center, says the official reports do not include untold numbers of undocumented Mexican workers in the area when the hijacked jets tore through the Twin Towers. I think the consulate is referring only to the executives of Mexican companies who have offices there. Let me tell you, there are a lot of restaurants at the World Trade Center. The majority of Mexicans in New York work in restaurants.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: Many of those undocumented workers likely came from this central part of Mexico. Their migration to New York City has helped send the Mexican population there soaring. 203% in the past decade. Mario Gonzaga arrived in New York 10 years ago. The morning the chaos fell on New York City, Gonzaga was at home in a mostly Mexican neighborhood in Queens, some 20 miles from Manhattan.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: Gonzaga says he called family members in the Mexican city of Puebla to tell them that he's alive, and that his taco restaurant in Queens was not harmed. Back in Mexico, television has been broadcasting phone numbers that people here can call to learn about the status of their loved ones in New York.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: President Vicente Fox has also taken to the airwaves to express solidarity with the US and support for Mexicans living in New York. I have given instructions to all our diplomatic representatives to redouble efforts and provide all the support necessary to our countrymen in the United States. Mexico's foreign minister has announced that Washington has Mexico's full backing if it decides to launch military reprisals for the attacks.

Many average Mexicans, meantime, have been praying for the victims' family members and for world peace. At the now heavily guarded US embassy, one woman left flowers and a lone candle in memory of the dead. For Latino USA, this is Franc Contreras in Mexico City.

Among the actions taken in the immediate aftermath of the terrorist attacks was an order for greater security along the borders with Mexico and Canada. Latino USA's Alex Avila reports that while some feel a greater focus on border security is long overdue, others fear the result will have a negative impact on cross-border trade. More than a million and a half people illegally crossed the Mexican and Canadian borders every day. So it was significant when on September 11, as television and radio stations flashed reports of the terrorist attacks in New York and Washington, a major cable network reported that the border had been closed.

In San Diego, California and Laredo, Texas, bomb threats did force the brief closure of six bridges, but says Nicole Chulick of the Border Patrol. The border was not shut down yesterday. There was misinformation. However. INS immigration officers and Border Patrol agents were at a heightened state of alert and remain at a heightened state of alert. The larger question of overall border security is not new.

For years, the border has been an area where contraband, drugs, and people have been illicitly smuggled back and forth. But with the dramatic increase in legitimate trade, some experts have worried that someone could smuggle in a major chemical, biological, or explosive weapon. Stephen Flynn is senior fellow at the National Security studies program on Foreign Relations. Earlier this summer at a US Mexico border summit in Edinburgh, Texas, Flynn warned that focusing on a possible missile attack is misguided. I would suggest that if I were a bad guy, I wouldn't invest in a ballistic missile. What I would do instead is I would put it in a truck. I would put it in a container. I would put it in a vehicle or vessel, and I'd simply sail it in across the border.

Flynn described one scenario for using the open border to carry out a major terrorist act. If bin Laden, the terrorist, contracted with me, and I can assure you he hasn't, I would suggest, perhaps, for instance, that what we might do is we'll buy out a company in Pakistan that's been bringing ceramics into the New York area for the last 30 years. But in one of the shipments, we'll put a chemical weapon and ship it to the Port of Long Beach, which means that we don't have to report what we're bringing, where it's from or where it's going for 30 days because it will travel in bond across the United States.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: And then I would suggest, maybe perhaps outside of Chicago and the rail station, because we moved from Long Beach to Chicago by rail, I might set the device off. Imagine if the commissioner of customs has to testify before Congress as a matter of routine, we allow 40 foot multi-ton containers to roam around the United States for 30 days at a whack without anybody telling us anything about them, because we're trying to facilitate trade.
From the general perspective of commerce and trade. I really think it's a stretch to say that a trade regulatory relaxation has anything to do with the ability to perpetrate terrorism.

Sam Vale is chair of the Strategic Planning Committee of the Border Trade Alliance. Sure, Vale says there's more traffic now, and increased traffic means more opportunities. But he says the number of front line inspectors hasn't kept up with increased trade. As much as we would like to say that we are capable of sustaining ourselves, I think everybody knows that today we are in a global economy. And just like you cannot cut off Texas from Oklahoma, you certainly cannot cut off Mexico from Canada or the US and expect to compete viably with the European Union or the Far East, or the MERCOSUR and Latin America.

Both Vale and Flynn say better enforcement procedures and more trained personnel would help to safeguard our borders. But what's needed most to protect the nation from terrorism, they say, is reliable intelligence. The lack of which many people blame for the carnage in New York and Washington. For Latino USA, I'm Alex Avila.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: Many people have compared the attacks in New York and Washington to the attack on Pearl Harbor, which launched the US into World War II. But Youth Radio commentator Sylvia Rivera says she prays that some of the mistakes of that war won't be repeated.

At the age of 20. I suddenly realized how fragile life is. How could someone create so much destruction? Perhaps I will never find the answers to this question. I can only share with others what I do know. When the smoke clears, we must rise from the ashes and rebuild our cities, our hearts and our minds. We must let the world know that our spirits are unshakable and that beliefs in freedom will never be destroyed.

Already I've heard a few comments that have shaken me to the core. That's why we have to be careful who we let in. We let too many foreigners into this country, and we should have bombed the Arabs a long time ago. These comments are dangerous. Let us not forget the injustices of World War II, when Japanese-Americans were placed in camps and ostracized for crimes they did not commit. Ethnic origin or religion are not our enemies here, terrorism is. We must support one another during this time, as we are all victims of this attack.

When the smoke clears, we must also clear our hearts of anger, seeking justice, not war. We must stand in solidarity no matter what race, gender, age, or religion. By keeping the principles of freedom alive, we honor those who perished so they did not die in vain. America, despite its many imperfections, is a land of liberty. As my generation copes with this moment, I find comfort that for once, we all stand on common ground. Let us continue to fight for the rights of all, taking a moment to pray not only for the well-being of our own country, but for all those countries who every day live with the fear of bombings, terrorism, and innocent death. We often hear these stories and think of them as somebody else's problem, until now.
Commentator Sylvia Rivera comes to us from Youth Radio. I was supposed to write an essay for this special edition of Latino USA,

but last night, September 12, when I finally got home at 10:00 PM, I realized that I just couldn't. I was completely exhausted and suddenly consumed with fear. The morning I heard of the terrorist explosions, I got on a subway to go down to the World Trade Center. I was going to report from there for CNN, but then I got stuck in the subway at 23rd Street. Maybe there was a reason why I shouldn't be going down there, I thought. Todo pasa por una razon.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: I emerged from the subway and Fifth Avenue was filled with people, everybody looking South, watching as the World Trade Centers burned. And then one tower crumbled. I started running down the streets crying.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: Before I went home last night, I stopped off at a fire engine house, engine house number 9 on 48th and 8th Avenue. There they lost 15 men. Many people were walking through the streets, stopping to leave flowers in front of the station house. That sense of New Yorkers wanting to do something, even if it was as little as lighting a candle. A Lebanese man came and left a postcard of the World Trade centers at the altar, and behind it he wrote from someone who knows what it's like to lose people.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: My thoughts are with you. An Argentinean woman who's lived in New York for 30 years went and hugged every single one of those firefighters. She told me that she just needed to touch them. I wouldn't be telling you the truth if I didn't say that I have been consumed with fear at some moments for my husband and my children. There's also been sadness, crying.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: But last night, watching television, I was most moved by the spirit of response. Down at ground zero yesterday, I saw people breaking out into moments of applause as the fire trucks and army trucks filed in to help in the rescue. People applauding, praying, giving their support to the rescue workers. People in New York City giving away free food, water.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: A guy who came from the South Bronx making coffee on a little electric burner because he just wanted to let them know that he cared. There is a void in New York City. We will feel it for a long time. I'm hoping that the void, the emptiness, is filled with New Yorkers coming together to help. This is Maria Hinojosa reporting.
